INTEREST OF THE AMICI CURIAE
Amici curiae are former presidentially appointed
United States Attorneys from three different
Administrations and 11 different judicial districts. 1
Each has experience prosecuting crimes in “Indian
country,” as defined by 18 U.S.C. § 1151. Specifically:
• Michael W. Cotter was appointed by
President Barack Obama as United States
Attorney for the District of Montana and
served from 2009 to 2017.
• Barry R. Grissom was appointed by
President Barack Obama as United States
Attorney for the District of Kansas and
served from 2010 to 2016.
• John W. Huber was appointed by President
Barack Obama and re-appointed by
President Donald Trump as United States
Attorney for the District of Utah and served
from 2015 to 2021.
• David C. Iglesias was appointed by
President George W. Bush as United States
Attorney for the District of New Mexico and
served from 2001 to 2007.
• Joe Kelly was appointed by President
Donald Trump as United States Attorney
for the District of Nebraska and served from
2018 to 2021.

1 No counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in
part, and no person other than amici curiae  or their counsel
made a monetary contribution to the preparation or submission
of this brief.

2


• Mark A. Klaassen was appointed by
President Donald Trump as United States
Attorney for the District of Wyoming and
served from 2017 to 2021.
• Brian J. Kuester was appointed by
President Donald Trump as United States
Attorney for the Eastern District of
Oklahoma and served from 2017 to 2021.
• Wendy J. Olson was appointed by President
Barack Obama as United States Attorney
for the District of Idaho and served from
2010 to 2017.
• Robert G. McCampbell was appointed by
President George W. Bush as United States
Attorney for the Western District of
Oklahoma and served from 2001 to 2005.
• Bryan D. Schroder was appointed by
President Donald Trump as United States
Attorney for the District of Alaska and
served from 2017 to 2021.
• R. Trent Shores was appointed by President
Donald Trump as United States Attorney
for the Northern District of Oklahoma and
served from 2017 to 2021.
• Danny C. Williams, Sr. was appointed by
President Barack Obama as United States
Attorney for the Northern District of
Oklahoma and served from 2012 to 2017.
As former United States Attorneys, Amici have
developed and implemented public safety initiatives
impacting tribal communities and/or Alaska Native
villages. Moreover, Amici have themselves prosecuted

3


and/or supervised the prosecution of violent crimes in
Indian country, including homicide, sexual assault,
and domestic violence. In doing so, Amici developed a
unique understanding of the tragic nexus between
substance abuse and violence in Native American and
Alaska Native communities. Amici understand the
gravity of the crime committed by Petitioner because
of its impact on a small, rural, and remote indigenous
community. As a result of their collective experience,
it is the position of the Amici that the forfeiture of
Petitioner’s plane is not an excessive fine because it is
proportional to the gravity of the offense he
committed. The Amici respectfully submit this brief to
offer former federal prosecut ors’ perspectives on why
the conveyance of alcohol into an Alaska Native
community that voted to exclude it is a serious offense
and why the judgment in this case is a proportionate
one.

SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
Petitioner argues the confiscation of a $95,000
airplane is disproportionate to his crime of
transporting allegedly only  a six-pack of beer. He
argues that the gravity of his offense must be
evaluated by reference to his own wrongdoing and
that blanket confiscation of an aircraft transporting
any amount of alcohol to a dry village violates the
Excessive Fines Clause. In addition to incorrectly
downplaying his own wrongdoing in this case,
Petitioner’s argument also ignores the important
public safety interests served by the Alaska statutory
scheme, which recognizes the danger that even small

4


amounts of alcohol may pose in remote Alaska villages
and the need to deter such conduct.
  Petitioner is a commercial air-taxi operator who
loaded nine gallons of beer into his aircraft for
delivery to Beaver, a Gwich’in village of fewer than
100 people on the Yukon River. The residents of
Beaver, which may be reached only by air, had voted
to prohibit the importation of alcohol. The jury found
that Petitioner knowingly allowed beer onto his
aircraft for the flight to Beaver, and the trial court
found that at least a six-pack sat in plain view of
Petitioner in an open grocery bag. Pet. App. 4a–5a, 7a,
33a. The Supreme Court of Alaska held that the
forfeiture the legislature has mandated for aircraft
transporting any amount of alcohol into a dry village
is not grossly disproportional to its gravity. That
judgment is correct for at least four reasons.
First, the Alaska Legislature’s decision to require
forfeiture of aircraft used  to carry any amount of
alcohol into dry villages was not an arbitrary one. It
was based on decades of studies documenting that
alcohol drives most violent crime in rural Alaska. The
statute was refined in 2004 to  adopt a tiered scheme
that reserves mandatory forfeiture of cars and boats
for aggravated cases while treating aircraft
differently. With this distinction, the legislature
recognized that aircraft provide the only way to reach
remote—and particularly vulnerable—villages like
Beaver. Thus, preventing importation of alcohol by air
is essential. Bajakajian instructs that judgments
about the appropriate punishment for an offense
belong to the legislature in the first instance. United
States v. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. 321, 336 (1998). Here,
the Alaska Legislature exercised its judgment to

5


address proven public safety concerns, and that
judgment is entitled to deference.
Second, the forfeiture of conveyances used to
introduce liquor into a Native community is not a new
concept. Congress has provided for it since the Trade
and Intercourse Act of 1834,  and it remains federal
law today, 18 U.S.C. § 3669, without regard to
quantity. Because most Alaska Native villages are not
Indian country, Alaska’s local-option statutes perform
in Alaska the important function federal law performs
elsewhere.
Third, the harm factor in Bajakajian asks about
the harm an offense causes and threatens, not the
price of the contraband. Nin e gallons of beer is a
different quantity in a village of 80 people than in a
city of 8,000, and the reco rd shows that Petitioner’s
practice of not looking at what his passengers carried
was known in the village s he served and had
consequences there. Measured against that harm, the
loss of the aircraft is severe but not grossly
disproportional, and the ratio between the forfeiture
and the authorized fines fa lls within the range this
Court and the lower courts have sustained.
Finally, the rule Petitioner asks the Court to adopt
would deprive dry villages of the one sanction that
reaches the people with the means to defeat their
choice. The judgment should be affirmed.

6


ARGUMENT
I. Petitioner committed a serious offense
that threatened public safety and
violated the will of the Alaska
Legislature and the Village of Beaver.
The proportionality inquiry requires consideration
of the gravity of the offense at issue. Bajakajian, 524
U.S. at 334, 337–39. Here, th e gravity of Petitioner’s
offense cannot be overstated.
A. The Alaska Legislature’s judgment rests
on a well-documented public-safety crisis
and is entitled to substantial deference.
The Alaska Legislature first enacted the local
option and forfeiture prov isions in 1980 following a
series of studies illustrating the strong connection
between alcohol-consumption and crime in rural
Alaskan villages. These studies, which are collected in
the opinions below, Pet. App. 83a–87a, found that in
rural Alaska, alcohol was linked to
• 77.9% of violent crimes;
• 64% of criminal homicides;
• 34% of forcible rapes;
• 41% of aggravated assaults; and
• 55.6% of property crimes.
See Harrison v. State , 687 P.2d 332, 335–36 (Alaska
App. 1984) (citing  Alaska Felony Sentences: 1976–
1979, at 45–48, 65–67 (1980)); Abraham v. State, 585
P.2d 526, 532 n.19 (Alaska 1978)  (citing report of the
National Council on Alcoholism).

7


When the legislature expanded the local option in
1986, including adding the forfeiture provisions, it
included a series of findings in the session law itself,
concluding that the dangers of alcohol abuse were
particularly acute in rural Alaska Native
communities because they are small and remote, often
lack adequate health care and law enforcement, and
cannot absorb the economic costs of alcohol abuse.
SLA 1986, ch. 80, § 1; Pet. App. 86a–87a, subsections
(2), (6), & (8).
Alaska’s local-option law has been effective in
increasing public safety. A study published in the
Journal of Studies on Alcohol  in 2000 found that
Alaska Native communities that banned alcohol had
markedly lower rates of homicide and accident-related
deaths than comparable communities that did not.
Matthew Berman, Teresa Hull & Philip May, Alcohol
Control and Injury Death in Alaska Native
Communities: Wet, Damp and Dry Under Alaska's
Local Option Law , 61 J. Stud. Alcohol 311 (2000). A
later study reported that the rates of serious injury
resulting from assault, motor-vehicle collisions, and
“other causes” were lower in dry villages than in
communities that continued to permit alcohol. Darryl
S. Wood & Paul J. Gruenewald, Local Alcohol
Prohibition, Police Presence and Serious Injury in
Isolated Alaska Native Villages , 101 Addiction 393
(2006).
None of these studies are surprising to the Amici.
Their experiences as prosecutors in Indian country
are consistent with these findings. For example,
alcohol played a role in the great majority of domestic
violence and sexual-assault cases their offices
prosecuted that involved Native perpetrators and/or

8


victims. And alcohol-fueled crimes in general are a
significant problem throughout Indian country.
But compared to the districts in which the non-
Alaskan Amici served, alcohol poses an even greater
threat to remote Alaska Native communities. As the
Alaska Legislature recognized, the isolation of the
villages exacerbates the impact of alcohol-induced
violence and accidents. Adequate healthcare is often
not available in rural Alaska. Moreover, many of the
communities lack regular access to law enforcement.
See Indian Law & Order Comm’n, A Roadmap for
Making Native America Safer ch. 2 (2013). In 2019, an
investigation by the Anchorage Daily News and
ProPublica found that one in three communities in
Alaska had no local law en forcement. K. Hopkins,
Lawless, Anchorage Daily News  (May 16, 2019). Of
those unprotected villages, 70 were large enough in
population to have both a school and a post office. Id.
Yet village residents who fell victim to a crime were
forced to wait for help to arrive by plane, boat, allterrain vehicle, or snowmobile. Id. Thus, for rural
Alaska Native communities, “unlike most anywhere
else in the United States, emergency help is hours or
even days away.” Id.
The Alaska Legislature recognized that although
remote villages can ban alcohol from their
communities, this ban is only effective if it can be
enforced. Because many villages lack the law
enforcement personnel needed to enforce the ban or
address the impacts of alcohol after it arrives, there is
even greater need to stop alcohol from entering dry
villages in the first place. Thus, the legislature
amended the statute to provide the ability to stop the

9


importation of alcohol into the villages by confiscating
aircraft, vessels, and vehicles used to subvert the ban.
In this amendment, the legislature recognized the
heightened threat aircraft pose to rural communities.
The legislature singled out aircraft for mandatory
forfeiture while conditioning the forfeiture of vehicles
and watercraft on aggravating circumstances. Pet.
App. 20a–22a. The more remote a village is, the more
vulnerable it is to the impact of alcohol and the more
likely it is that alcohol will arrive via air. The pilot
who carries it is the gatekeeper, and a legislature that
places its strongest sanction at the gate has responded
to the problem rationally.
B. Local option is the Village’s own act of
self-governance.
A dry village is dry becaus e its residents voted to
make it so. Alaska Stat. § 04.11.491. Beaver’s ban was
not imposed from Juneau; it is the community’s own
judgment about how best to protect itself. When a
pilot from Fairbanks carries  alcohol into Beaver, he
does more than violate a state statute. He overrides a
decision the community made for itself, and the harm
that flows from that violation falls directly on
community members. Prosecutors who work with
tribal communities understand the difference
between a regulatory violation and a violation of a
community’s self-determination. The Alaska
Legislature understood it, too: the forfeiture provision
was enacted, in Judge Mannh eimer’s words, “to give
teeth” to the communities’ efforts. Pet. App. 86a.
Petitioner’s conduct defied those community efforts,
and the seriousness of the penalty should reflect the
gravity of his crime.

10


***
“[J]udgments about the appropriate punishment
for an offense belong in the first instance to the
legislature,” Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 336, and
reviewing courts “should grant substantial deference
to the broad authority that legislatures necessarily
possess in determining the types and limits of
punishments for crimes.” Solem v. Helm , 463 U.S.
277, 290 (1983). That deferenc e is owed most where,
as here, the legislature has acted on a record of local
harm and tailored the punishment to the threats
presented in a unique environment. This is
particularly true where the local community has
expressly invoked the protection offered by the
statute. Courts sitting fa r from rural Alaska are
poorly positioned to second-guess these decisions.
II. Federal law has long required forfeiture of
conveyances used to introduce liquor into
Native communities.
A. Congress has authorized forfeiture of
such conveyances since 1834.
“The protection against excessive fines has been a
constant shield throughout Anglo-American history.”
Timbs v. Indiana , 586 U.S. 146, 153 (2019). This
Court has looked to historic al practice in considering
whether violations of the Excessive Fines Clause have
occurred. See Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 330–32, 335;
Austin v. United States, 509 U.S. 602, 611–18 (1993).
Such practice supports the forfeiture provisions
adopted by the Alaska Legislature here.
From the early days of the Republic, Congress
prohibited the introduction of liquor into Indian

11


country. The Trade and Intercourse Act of 1834 made
it unlawful to introduce liquor or wine into Indian
country and authorized officers to search the “boats,
stores, packages, and places of deposit” of any person
suspected of doing so and to  seize, for forfeiture, any
liquor or wine found. Act of  June 30, 1834, ch. 161, §
20, 4 Stat. 729, 732. Like th e Alaska statute, the Act
was later amended to extend the forfeiture to “the
boats, teams, wagons, and sleds used in conveying”
liquor and wine. Act of March 15, 1864, ch. 33, 13 Stat.
29. That policy has remained in force for nearly two
centuries. Today, it is codified in 18 U.S.C. §§ 1154
and 1156, which criminalize dispensing or possessing
intoxicants in Indian country, and in 18 U.S.C. § 3669,
which provides that any conveyance used by any
person “in introducing or attempting to introduce
intoxicants into the Indian country” is “subject to
seizure, libel, and forfeiture.” The federal statute, like
Alaska’s, applies to any quantity of alcohol.
The federal scheme rests on the judgment the
Alaska Legislature later made for itself: that the
conveyance should be forfeited because it makes the
introduction of alcohol into an isolated community
possible, and future alcohol transfers cannot occur in
a vehicle that has been forfeited. A sanction Congress
has imposed without interruption since the Lincoln
Administration, and that this Court has treated as
unremarkable, is not the sort of penalty the Eighth
Amendment was ratified to forbid.
B. Alaska’s local-option statutes perform
in Alaska the function federal law
performs elsewhere.
The federal statutes criminalizing the importation
of alcohol into Indian country have limited reach in

12


Alaska. In Alaska v. Native Villa ge of Venetie Tribal
Government, 522 U.S. 520 (1998), this Court held that
lands conveyed under the Alaska Native Claims
Settlement Act are generally not “Indian country”
within the meaning of 18 U.S.C. § 1151. Like Beaver,
Venetie is a Gwich’in village in interior Alaska. Based
on this ruling, the federal prohibition on introducing
liquor into Indian country, and the federal forfeiture
that accompanies it, do not protect most Alaska
Native villages. However, the State’s local-option law
does. It gives a village the authority to adopt, by vote,
the same protection Congress has extended to tribal
communities elsewhere, and its forfeiture provision
supplies the same enforcement mechanism. The
statutes at issue are Alaska’s counterpart to
longstanding federal law and incorporate remedies
that have been imposed for similar crimes for almost
two centuries.
Forfeiture of a conveyance used to carry
contraband is among the oldest forms of forfeiture in
the United States.  See Bennis v. Michigan,  516 U.S.
442, 446–49 (1996); Calero-Toledo v. Pearson Yacht
Leasing Co., 416 U.S. 663, 680–86 (1974). The Court
need not decide whether every such forfeiture
survives Eighth Amendment scrutiny to conclude that
this one does.

13


III. Measured against the harm the
offense threatens, forfeiture of
Petitioner’s aircraft is not grossly
disproportional.
A. The gravity of the offense turns on
the harm it threatens, not the
market value of the contraband.
The retail value of the alcohol on Petitioner’s plane
says little about the gravity of his offense. What
matters is what his co nduct threatened: the
transportation of alcohol into a community that has
determined, based on its own experience and
circumstances, that it cannot safely bear the harms
associated with it. Th at approach tracks Bajakajian,
which rejected any “inherent proportionality” between
the dollar amount involved in an offense and the harm
it causes. 524 U.S. at 339.
There, the Court found the harm caused by the
offense to be “minimal” because the defendant’s
conduct “affected only one party, the Government, and
in a relatively minor way.” Id. The Court identified
several other features that made the offense
minimally harmful: it was “solely a reporting offense,”
unrelated to any other illegal activity, and the
defendant was not among the offenders the statute
was “principally designed” to reach. Id. at 337–38.
The offense here bears none of those features. It is
not a technical reporting violation affecting the
Government alone. Rather, it is the knowing
introduction of alcohol into a community that
deliberately chose to prohibit it—the precise conduct
the statute was designed to reach. See Alaska Stat. §
04.11.499(a), (c)(3). The harms the legislature

14


identified, which include vi olence, injury, and death,
are particularly severe in small, remote villages,
where limited police and medical resources leave
communities less able to prevent or respond to them.
See Pet. App. 24a-25a, 86a– 87a. The gravity of
Petitioner’s offense therefor e lies not in the value of
the contraband, but in the substantial harm his
conduct threatened to bring into the community.2
Nor can the quantity of alcohol be assessed apart
from the community for which it was destined.
Seventy-two cans of beer may be insignificant against
the population and infrastructure of Fairbanks. But
in Beaver—a village of less than 100 people—the
same quantity represents a substantial supply.
Beaver’s isolation compounds the consequences: there
are no roads in or out of the village, and the nearest
hospital is in Fairbanks, more than 100 miles away.
Resp. Br. at 12. These circumstances bear directly on
the harm the legislature—and Beaver itself—sought
to prevent and thus on the gravity the State
reasonably attributed to the transportation of alcohol
into such a community.
Finally, Petitioner was squarely within the
category of offenders the statute was designed to

2 That troopers intercepted the alcohol before the aircraft left
Fairbanks does not diminish the gravity of the offense.
Bajakajian itself measured harm by asking what the offense
would have accomplished had it succeeded, observing that if the
defendant’s crime had “gone undetected, the Government would
have been deprived only of the information that $357,144 had
left the country.” 524 U.S. at 339.  And critically, Petitioner’s
offense of conviction includes attempted delivery, not merely
completed delivery. Alaska Stat. § 04.11.499(c)(1), (3). An offense
stopped at the airstrip is therefore no less grave than one
completed.

15


reach. Troopers watched him open and close boxes
while loading the aircraft, with a six-pack of beer
sitting unsecured in a grocery bag and plainly visible
through the plane’s wind ow. Pet. App. 4a, 33a.  The
jury was instructed that knowledge includes
deliberate ignorance, and it convicted him on these
facts. Pet. App. 5a. A pilot who chooses to remain
ignorant of his cargo becomes the carrier of choice for
passengers who intend to bring alcohol into a dry
community. The forfeiture provision was intended to
stop this conduct by targeting people like Petitioner
who facilitated the transport of alcohol into dry
villages and eliminating the means by which they
could accomplish it.
B. The ratio between the forfeiture and
the authorized penalties is within
the range courts have sustained.
The Alaska Legislature did not leave forfeiture to
the happenstance of an individual sentencing
decision. It made forfeiture of aircraft mandatory
when the statutory conditions  are met, reflecting its
judgment that removing the means of transportation
is necessary to deter the very conduct at issue here.
The statute’s history reinforces that judgment. See
Pet. App. 20a–22a. And the ra tio of forfeiture to the
authorized penalties at is sue here falls comfortably
within the range that courts applying Bajakajian
have sustained.
Indeed, Petitioner’s aircraft was worth
approximately nine and a half times the $10,000
maximum fine Petitioner faced. Pet. App. 7a n.10. The
forfeiture in Bajakajian, by contrast, was more than
70 times the maximum fine under the Sentencing
Guidelines. 524 U.S. at 338–39 & n.14. The

16


comparison is starker still for KenAir, Petitioner’s codefendant and the company that operated the aircraft,
which faced a maximum fine of $500,000—more than
five times the value of the plane. Pet. App. 7a n.10.
Courts applying Bajakajian have sustained
forfeitures at—and above—the ratio presented here.
See Pet. App. 23a n.89 (colle cting cases, including
United States v. Castello , 611 F.3d 116, 123 (2d Cir.
2010), and United States v. Mackby , 339 F.3d 1013,
1016–19 (9th Cir. 2003)).
Moreover, Petitioner’s sentence included jail time,
a $3,000 fine with $1,500 suspended, three years of
probation, and other conditions prohibiting him from
carrying alcohol into any dry village. Pet. App. 5a. The
court specifically stated that it did not impose
forfeiture alongside these penalties lightly. Id. The
forfeiture therefore was not an anomalous
punishment imposed alongside an otherwise minimal
sentence, unlike in Bajakajian, where the maximum
available penalties “confirm[ed] a minimal level of
culpability.” 524 U.S. at 339.
C. The record does not show that
forfeiture deprived Petitioner of his
livelihood.
Bajakajian did not reach whether a forfeiture’s
effect on the defendant’s livelihood bears on
proportionality. 524 U.S. at  340 n.15. But even if it
does, the record provides no basis for finding that the
forfeiture deprived Petitioner of his livelihood.
Petitioner owned a second ai rcraft, also used by his
company, and flew it to Beaver on the same day the
first was seized. Pet. A pp. 27a. And at a postconviction evidentiary hearing, Petitioner testified
that he was “pretty much retired” and would

17


“probably just sell” the aircraft  if it were returned to
him. Pet. App. 26a-27a. Livelihood therefore lends no
support to a finding of gross disproportionality.
IV. Petitioner’s proposed rule would
disable the sanction that protects
dry villages.
Petitioner argues the Alaska Supreme Court
“viewed the gravity of [his] error purely in the
abstract,” and he (incorrectly) characterizes his error
as merely transporting a six-pack of beer. Pet. Br. 40.
According to Petitioner, forfeiture is impermissible
under the statute if the am ount of alcohol to be
transported is low enough. Rather than the brightline
and no-exceptions policy enacted by the Alaska
Legislature and embraced by the people of Beaver,
Petitioner’s rule would leave open the question of how
much alcohol is enough to warrant confiscation. Such
a rule would tell every operator who flies into a dry
village that transporting a six pack–or maybe two or
three—risks only minor punishment, not confiscation
of their aircraft. It would tell every village that a
major sanction it relied on when it voted to go dry is
no longer available. It would convert a mandatory
forfeiture into a mandatory evidentiary hearing about
how much is too much alcohol and what a passenger
did, or could have done, with it. And it would do so on
the premise that a court in Washington or Anchorage
is better placed than the Alaska Legislature and the
voters of Beaver to weigh the danger of 72 beers—or
even a six-pack—in a remote village of less than 100
people.
This Court has not read the Excessive Fines
Clause to require such a result. The Clause guards
against fines that are “grossly disproportional to the

18


gravity of a defendant’s offense.” Bajakajian, 524 U.S.
at 334. The Court has emphasized that successful
proportionality challenges outside the capital
punishment context should be “exceedingly rare,”
Rummel v. Estelle , 445 U.S. 263, 272 (1980); see
Solem, 463 U.S. at 290 n.16. The forfeiture of an
aircraft used by a commercial pilot to carry alcohol
into a community that lawfully excluded it—under a
statute that has required such a forfeiture for decades
and that mirrors a federal policy nearly two centuries
old—is neither rare nor aberrational. It is the sanction
the people most affected ha ve chosen, applied to the
people best positioned to prevent the harm.
Amici do not suggest that the Clause has no
application to forfeitures or that a legislature may
declare any property used in any offense forfeitable
without limit. Timbs settled that the Clause applies
to the States, and Bajakajian settled that it has
content. The point is narrower. Where a legislature
has acted on a documented record of harm to protect
a vulnerable population, has calibrated its remedy
across offenses and conveyances, has preserved
protection for innocent owners, and has chosen a
sanction with deep roots in the Nation’s law, the
Eighth Amendment does not permit a court to
displace that judgment because the offender’s
contraband, viewed in isol ation, may appear small.
